summary: This unit teaches you to judge whether a new technology is right for a business before money is spent. You will learn to start from the business problem, list requirements, compare options by total cost of ownership, return on investment, payback and weighted scoring, assess risks such as security, supplier failure, power and internet outages and lock-in, test by pilot or proof of concept, write a clear recommendation and review results after the system goes live.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. New technology arrives constantly: cloud software, mobile apps, contactless payments, automation, artificial intelligence. Some of it can transform a business. Some of it wastes money, disrupts staff and exposes customer data. The manager's job is not to chase every new tool but to **evaluate** it: to decide, with evidence, whether it will solve a real business problem at a cost and risk the business can accept.

Jamaican businesses face particular conditions that an evaluation must include: power cuts and weak internet in some areas, small budgets, an exchange rate that affects the cost of imported systems and licences, and a data protection law that sets rules for personal data.
**Who it is for:** managers and senior supervisors who recommend or approve technology purchases or changes, such as new software, equipment or online services.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with business scenarios and calculations.
A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms and quick sums) and longer answers.

**Group practicals**: evaluating three technology options and writing a recommendation report; and running a proof-of-concept test of an online tool and presenting a go or no-go decision. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice and write the formula first. Say whether you are using a purchase price or a total over a period.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The most common mistake is to fall in love with a product, for example an app seen at a trade show, and then look for a use for it. The right first step is to **define the business problem** the technology should solve.

flow: Describe the problem or opportunity (what is going wrong or could be better, and how you know)
Set measurable goals (for example cut stock-outs by half, serve customers in two minutes)
List requirements and rank them as must-have or nice-to-have
Scan the market for options that could meet them
Shortlist and compare
Test, decide, introduce and review

head: Type
Examples
rows: Record sales, track stock in six branches, issue invoices, take bookings
Work with our accounts and payment systems; run on the phones our staff use; work offline
Handle double the transactions in two years
Protect personal data; keep records as the law requires

blocks.note: A **must-have** is a requirement without which the system is no use. A **nice-to-have** adds value but can be done without. Use the must-haves first to remove unsuitable options.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Even when current systems work, a business should **regularly scan for new technologies** to spot changes that could bring gains or threats, such as a competitor who offers online booking. Scanning does not mean buying; it means knowing what is out there and deciding when to act.

blocks.note: When you read that a new technology "will transform every business", look for **evidence of results in similar firms**. Treat claims as questions to test, not as facts.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The people who will use the system know the daily tasks it must support. Involve them in drawing up requirements, in the trial and in the choice. A system that fits the work is more likely to be used.
You do not need to be a technician, but you must understand the main models well enough to ask the right questions.

Cloud / SaaS
On-premises

Needs a connection; plan offline use and backup power

blocks.p: Neither is always better. A small firm with limited IT staff often benefits from SaaS and its lower upfront cost and professional security, provided the internet and power are reliable and the contract is sound. A firm in an area with weak internet may need a system that works offline and synchronises later.

A newer product may have more features but fewer users, less support and more bugs. A proven product has a track record, wider support and a lower risk. For a **small firm with limited IT staff**, the proven option is usually wiser when scores are close.
Avoid buying a system built on technology that is being phased out across the industry. It may soon lack support, updates and compatible equipment, and have to be replaced early.
The purchase price is only part of the cost. The **total cost of ownership (TCO)** is the full cost of a system over its life.

head: Cost
Examples
rows: Courses, staff time away from work
Moving old records into the new system, and cleaning them
Staff time lost while learning, temporary slowdown, extra staff to run both systems for a while, extra security
The cost of getting data out and moving later

blocks.p: **Example 1.** A system costs J$800,000 to buy, J$200,000 to install and J$150,000 a year for support. Over 3 years: 800,000 + 200,000 + (3 × 150,000) = 1,000,000 + 450,000 = **J$1,450,000**.

**Example 2: cloud or server over 3 years.** Cloud service: J$30,000 a month × 36 months = **J$1,080,000**. Server: J$900,000 to buy + J$120,000 a year × 3 years = 900,000 + 360,000 = **J$1,260,000**. The cloud service is cheaper by 1,260,000 − 1,080,000 = **J$180,000**. Check: 1,080,000 + 180,000 = 1,260,000.
**Example 3: licences.** 25 users at J$3,000 per user per month: 25 × 3,000 = J$75,000 a month, and × 12 = **J$900,000 a year**.
**Example 4: average yearly cost.** A system with a five-year TCO of J$2,500,000 averages 2,500,000 ÷ 5 = **J$500,000 a year**.

blocks.note: When comparing options, use the **same period** for all of them and include **every** cost. Do not compare one option's purchase price with another's monthly fee.
blocks.label: Remember

Examples

4 minutes saved on each of 900 documents: 3,600 minutes = 60 hours
Yes, then multiply by the staff hourly cost

blocks.p: Check: 35% of 1,000,000 is 350,000, so benefits are 1,350,000. 24 × 75,000 = 1,800,000. A short payback is attractive, but also consider the **life** of the system: a payback of 24 months on a system that lasts 6 years is much better than on one that lasts 3.
When many factors matter, use a **weighted scoring matrix** so that the factors count in proportion to their importance. Agree the criteria and the weights first, and the weights must add to 100%.
Do the same for each option and compare the totals. If two totals are very close, do not decide on the score alone; check risks, references and a trial.

A growing business with little spare cash may evaluate **leasing or a subscription**, which spread the cost over time and protect cash flow, against buying outright, which can cost less overall. Compare both the total cost and the effect on cash each month.
Every technology brings risk. List them in a **risk register** with likelihood and impact, controls, an owner and a review date. Include at least the following.

blocks.p: A **service level agreement (SLA)** sets out agreed standards, such as uptime and response times, and what happens if the provider fails to meet them.

head: Uptime promised
Allowed downtime in a 30-day month (720 hours)
How worked out

blocks.p: A figure that looks high, such as 99%, still allows hours of downtime in a month. Ask whether that suits your business.
Open-source software may be free to download, but you must still plan for **set-up, support, training and updates**. Free to get is not the same as free to run.

Software that records every keystroke or listens to staff meetings raises questions of **privacy, the law, trust and consultation**. An artificial intelligence tool can be wrong or unfair. Test its accuracy, tell the people affected, protect data and keep a person responsible for decisions that affect staff or customers.

Meaning

A credit union asks a vendor to set up a small version of its app before signing a three-year contract

flow: Decide what you want to find out and the success measures
Record a baseline: how long the tasks take now, and how many errors
Set up the trial with a small group, using real or realistic data
Run the test tasks and record time, problems and screenshots
Collect feedback from the users
Compare with the baseline and the success measures
Decide: go, go with changes, or no-go

blocks.note: Use made-up or test data for a trial wherever possible. Do not put real personal data into a tool that has not passed your checks.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Ask for **references from existing customers** of similar size, and ask how well the system and the support met their needs.
Check the company's history, financial stability and number of customers.
See a demonstration of your own tasks, not just a general one.
Ask about support hours, response times and where support is based.
Ask about the roadmap and about how often the product is updated.

blocks.p: Before signing, check:

ul: **Who owns the data** and how it is returned or deleted if you leave.
The SLA: uptime, response, remedies.
Length of contract, price changes, renewal and exit terms.
Security and data protection commitments.
What is included: training, support, updates, backups.
Licences: how many users, what happens if you add more.

blocks.p: Where possible, have the contract reviewed by a lawyer.

blocks.p: A report to the board should contain **the need, the options, the costs, the risks and a recommendation**.

sections.title: Introducing the technology and reviewing results

flow: Approve the budget and appoint a project owner
Confirm the plan with the vendor: dates, roles, data migration
Prepare the data and the people
Train staff before go-live, and have help on hand afterwards
Go live in stages where possible, with a fallback
Support users and fix problems quickly
Review results

blocks.p: A system that was well chosen can still fail if people are not trained or supported. When staff keep using paper rosters after a new scheduling system arrives, what was most likely missing was **training and change support**.
After the board approves a new system, tell staff **why it was chosen, what will change and what training will be given**. Listen to their concerns and answer questions.

Some months after go-live (often six), hold a planned **post-implementation review**. **Compare actual results with the business case**: costs, benefits, time saved, errors, user satisfaction and risks. Record what worked, what did not and what to do about it. Use the lessons for the next technology decision.

blocks.p: Plan for disasters: a fire, hurricane or cyber attack. Keep backups away from the main site, test restoring them, and have a **disaster recovery plan** that says how key systems and data will be restored and who is responsible.

terms: TCO
Total cost of ownership: the full cost of a system over its life
ROI
Return on investment: net gain divided by cost, as a percentage
Payback period
The time taken for savings to repay the cost
SaaS
Software as a service: software used online for a regular fee
IaaS
Infrastructure as a service: rented computing power, storage and networks
Cloud
Computing services delivered over the internet
On-premises
Software and servers owned and run on the business's own site
Open-source software
Software whose source code anyone may use, change and share
API
A software link that lets two systems exchange data
Integration
How well a new system works with existing ones
Scalability
The ability to handle more users or transactions as the business grows
SLA
Service level agreement: the provider's promised standards, such as uptime
Vendor lock-in
Being unable to move to another provider without high cost
Proof of concept
A small working version used to test whether the idea works
Pilot
A real trial in part of the business
Weighted scoring matrix
A comparison table in which each criterion has a weight
Data migration
Moving existing records from an old system into a new one
Hidden cost
A cost that does not appear on a supplier's invoice, such as staff time
Post-implementation review
A planned review some months after go-live
Disaster recovery plan
A plan for restoring key systems and data after a fire, hurricane or cyber attack

c1.title: A prep school's records system
c1.text: A private prep school in Portmore is choosing a system for student records and fee payments, to be used for 5 years. A cloud service costs J$30,000 a month, with set-up included. Buying a server costs J$900,000, plus J$120,000 a year for maintenance. The records include children's names and addresses. The school has power cuts several times a month, and the internet is sometimes slow.

c2.title: A bakery group compares three stock systems
c2.text: A bakery group in St Elizabeth has three quotations for a stock system. It scores each out of 10 on cost, ease of use and support, with weights of 30%, 40% and 30%. System A scores 8, 6 and 7. System B scores 6, 9 and 6. System C scores 9, 5 and 8.

c3.title: Barcode scanning at a Montego Bay distributor
c3.text: A distributor in Montego Bay will spend J$1,500,000 in total on a barcode scanning system for its warehouse. It expects to save J$75,000 a month and will use it for 3 years. Scanning saves 4 minutes on each batch of 900 picks. The manager has not included the cost of moving old stock records into the new system.

c4.title: A fishing cooperative's online ordering app
c4.text: A fishing cooperative in Old Harbour is considering an app for recording catches and selling to hotels. The provider promises 99.5% uptime in a 30-day month of 720 hours. The beach landing site has weak mobile signal and the power often fails. Many members are older and use basic phones. The contract does not say who owns the sales data.

c5.title: An AI note-taking tool for HR meetings
c5.text: The HR department of a Kingston insurance company wants to use an artificial intelligence tool that records and summarises meetings, including disciplinary and grievance meetings. The vendor says it is 'highly accurate' and can store recordings on servers overseas. Staff have not been told about the plan.

questions.q: What is the five-year cost of the cloud service?
What is the five-year cost of buying and maintaining the server?
questions.why: Purchase 900,000 + (5 × 120,000 maintenance) = 900,000 + 600,000 = J$1,500,000. The purchase price alone leaves out the running cost.

questions.q: On cost alone, which option is cheaper over five years, and by how much?
o: The cloud, by J$300,000
The server, by J$300,000
The server, by J$600,000
The cloud, by J$600,000
questions.why: 1,800,000 − 1,500,000 = 300,000 in favour of the server over five years. The answer depends on the period (over three years the cloud would be cheaper), and on non-money factors such as power and data protection.

questions.q: The records hold children's personal details. What is the most important check about the cloud provider?
o: Whether the provider's website looks professional
How the data is protected and who can see it
How many staff the provider employs in Jamaica
Whether the provider offers a longer free trial
questions.why: Personal data about children is sensitive, so the school must meet the data protection law's rules: security, access, location and use.

questions.q: Given the power cuts and slow internet, which feature should the school look for?
o: Offline working that syncs later, plus backup power
A longer contract with a lower monthly fee
A bigger screen on every office computer
Fewer passwords, so that staff can log in faster
questions.why: An online system fails when power or internet fails. Offline mode, backup power and a second line keep the school running.

questions.q: What is System A's weighted score?
questions.why: (8 × 0.30) + (6 × 0.40) + (7 × 0.30) = 2.4 + 2.4 + 2.1 = 6.9. Check: the weights add to 100%, so the result stays on the 10-point scale.

questions.q: Which system has the highest weighted score?
o: System A, with 6.9
System C, with 7.1
System B, with 7.2
Systems B and C tie
questions.why: B: 1.8 + 3.6 + 1.8 = 7.2. C: 2.7 + 2.0 + 2.4 = 7.1. A: 6.9. B is highest, but only narrowly.

questions.q: Why does the group weight the criteria instead of simply adding the scores?
o: Because weighting makes the final totals larger
Because the cheapest option must always win
Because some criteria matter more than others
Because the supplier normally requires it
questions.why: Weights make each criterion count in proportion to its importance. Here ease of use matters most, so it carries 40%.

questions.q: B and C are within 0.1 points. What should the group do next?
o: Pick B because it has the higher number
Run a trial and check references and risks
Pick C because it has a lower price
Pick the system with the best-looking screens
questions.why: A close score is not a decisive difference. A pilot, reference checks and a risk assessment give the evidence to separate them.

questions.q: What are the system's total benefits over the 3 years?
questions.why: 75,000 × 36 months = J$2,700,000. The net gain, after the J$1,500,000 cost, is J$1,200,000. Do not confuse benefits with net gain.

questions.q: What is the ROI over the 3 years?
How many staff hours does the scanning save per batch of 900 picks (4 minutes each)?
o: 15 hours
36 hours
3,600 hours
60 hours
questions.why: 4 × 900 = 3,600 minutes; 3,600 ÷ 60 = 60 hours. The 3,600 is minutes, not hours.

questions.q: The manager left out the cost of moving the old stock records. What does this mean for her estimate?
o: The cost is lower, so the payback is shorter
Nothing changes, as data migration is not a cost
The true cost is higher and the payback longer
The ROI must be higher than first calculated
questions.why: Data migration is a real cost that is often missed. Adding it raises total cost, lengthens payback and lowers ROI.

questions.q: What is the longest downtime the provider's 99.5% promise allows in the 30-day month?
o: 3.6 minutes
216 minutes
36 minutes
432 minutes
questions.why: 0.5% × 720 hours = 3.6 hours, which is 3.6 × 60 = 216 minutes. Check: 99.5% + 0.5% = 100%.

questions.q: Given the weak mobile signal and power failures at the landing site, which feature matters most?
o: Offline recording that syncs when the signal returns
Daily price alerts for hotel buyers and chefs
A longer free trial period for all members
Photographs of every catch in high resolution
questions.why: If the app needs a connection to record a catch, it will fail where the catch is landed. Offline recording that syncs later fits the site's conditions.

questions.q: The contract does not say who owns the sales data. What should the cooperative do before signing?
o: Have it say the cooperative owns and can export the data
Sign anyway, since data ownership is a minor detail
Accept that the provider will own all of the data
Ask only for a lower monthly price and sign
questions.why: Unclear data ownership leads to lock-in. The contract should say who owns the data and how it is returned if the cooperative leaves.

questions.q: Many members are older and use basic phones. What should the evaluation include?
o: Design for smartphone users only, as most buyers use them
Require all members to buy new phones at their own cost
Leave older members to find help on their own
Testing with these users, with training or a simpler option
questions.why: A system must fit the people who will use it. Test it with older members, provide training or an alternative channel, and check it runs on basic phones.

questions.q: What should the HR department do first before choosing the AI tool?
o: Buy the tool for a trial and tell the staff later
Rely on the vendor's claim that it is highly accurate
Define the purpose, check the law and consult staff
Record every meeting so that staff get used to it
questions.why: Meetings about discipline and grievances involve very sensitive personal data. The evaluation must weigh privacy, the law, trust and consultation before any purchase.

questions.q: The vendor stores recordings on servers overseas. What is the key point to check?
o: Whether the servers are kept in a cool climate
Whether overseas storage meets the data protection law
Whether the vendor has a large head office
Whether the recordings are in high definition
questions.why: Sending personal data to another country is allowed only if the law's conditions are met. The company must check this and the provider's safeguards.

questions.q: A proof of concept is planned. What data should the company use at first?
o: Real disciplinary meetings so the results are realistic
Made-up or test meetings, not real staff cases
Recordings of directors' private discussions
Whatever the vendor suggests
questions.why: Test with data that harms no one if something goes wrong. Real personal data should only be used once privacy and legal checks have been passed.
